explanations.explanation: She says, “Listen! My beloved approaches. Look! Here he comes, leaping across the mountains, bounding over the hills.” Mountains, friend. I get winded hopping over a bag of flour. Her beloved treats a whole mountain range like a speed bump.

No chariot shows up anywhere in these verses. She sees him coming on his own two feet, and those feet are busy. She says he is “leaping across the mountains, bounding over the hills.” That's not a ride, that's a workout.

A road sounds calm, but that's not what she sings. She says he is “leaping across the mountains, bounding over the hills.” Nobody leaps over a hill on the way to the mailbox. This man is in a HURRY to get to her.

explanations.answer: Arise and come away with him
explanations.explanation: That's it. He calls to her, “Arise, my darling. Come away with me, my beautiful one.” He isn't asking her to stay put. He wants her up and out the door with him.

He's already standing at the lattice, so there's no returning to wait for. What he says is, “Arise, my darling. Come away with me, my beautiful one.” That's an invitation to get up and go. Staying in is the opposite of what he's asking.

explanations.answer: Wait for him at the city gate
explanations.explanation: No gate in this call, friend. He's right outside her window, so there's nothing to wait for. He says, “Arise, my darling. Come away with me, my beautiful one.” He wants her to come with him right now.

He says, “The flowers have appeared in the countryside; the season of singing has come, and the cooing of turtledoves is heard in our land.” Winter's over, the rain's gone, and the whole countryside is warming up its voice. I think even the turtledoves are showing off a little.
Rest isn't what he calls it. He says, “the season of singing has come.” The winter and the rain are behind them, and now the land is making music. Nobody's napping in this verse.
This one points the other way, friend. He says, “For now the winter is past; the rain is over and gone.” Then he adds, “the season of singing has come.” Mourning has no place in this springtime.

Not quite, friend. Her beloved says, “The fig tree ripens its figs; the blossoming vines spread their fragrance.” That tree is not bare. It's in full springtime swing, and the vines are making the whole place smell wonderful.

Right, it's false. He says, “The fig tree ripens its figs; the blossoming vines spread their fragrance.” The tree is busy ripening figs, and the vines are blossoming. Winter is over and everything is waking up.
True! The voice says, “let me see your face, let me hear your voice.” He doesn't want her hiding up in the rocks. He adds, “for your voice is sweet, and your countenance is lovely.”

It's true, friend. The one calling says, “let me see your face, let me hear your voice.” He wants both, her face and her voice. He gives his reason too: “for your voice is sweet, and your countenance is lovely.”

Close, but the text says otherwise. The call is to catch “the little foxes that ruin the vineyards,” and then comes the reason: “for our vineyards are in bloom.” The vineyards are blooming, not ruined. The point is to stop the damage before it starts.

Right, it's false. The text says, “Catch for us the foxes—the little foxes that ruin the vineyards—for our vineyards are in bloom.” The vineyards are blooming, not ruined. Catch those foxes now, while there's still something to protect.

explanations.answer: She and her beloved belong to each other
explanations.explanation: She says, “My beloved is mine and I am his.” Short, sweet and no wasted words. Then she adds that he “pastures his flock among the lilies.”

explanations.answer: She and her beloved are still strangers
explanations.explanation: Strangers don't talk like this, friend. She says, “My beloved is mine and I am his.” That's two people who know exactly where they stand with each other.

explanations.answer: Her beloved is too far above her
explanations.explanation: She never says anything like that. She sings, “My beloved is mine and I am his.” That's not one person looking up at another. It's two people who belong to each other.

She says, “Before the day breaks and shadows flee, turn, my beloved, and be like a gazelle or a young stag on the mountains of Bether.” The clock is the sunrise. Mountains of Bether is a place named right there in her song. I think she wants every minute before the light comes.
Winter was already called past and gone back in verse 11. Her deadline is different: “Before the day breaks and shadows flee.” It's about the morning, not the seasons.
Harvest isn't mentioned in her request. She says, “Before the day breaks and shadows flee, turn, my beloved.” Her deadline is daybreak, so the sunrise is the clock.
Not this time, friend. She says, “On my bed at night I sought the one I love; I sought him, but did not find him.” She looked and he wasn't there. That's why the song takes a turn here.
Right, it's false. She says, “I sought him, but did not find him.” She's on her bed at night, looking, and he isn't there. I think that's a long, quiet kind of night.

explanations.answer: Gets up and searches the city
explanations.explanation: She says, “I will arise now and go about the city, through the streets and squares. I will seek the one I love.” She doesn't lie there hoping. She puts her feet on the floor and goes.
She doesn't wait for sunrise. She says, “I will arise now and go about the city, through the streets and squares.” The word is now. That's not someone planning to sleep on it.

explanations.answer: Calls out to him from her window
explanations.explanation: No window shouting here, friend. She says, “I will arise now and go about the city, through the streets and squares.” She goes out to look for him herself.
She says, “I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city.” They were walking their route and she walked right into them. Nobody knows a city at night like the people paid to patrol it.
Temple guards aren't in this scene. She says, “I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city.” These are the ones walking the city streets.
Shepherds showed up earlier, when he pastured his flock among the lilies. Out in the city at night, she says, “I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city.” Different crew, different job.
She asks, “Have you seen the one I love?” It's a simple question. She's out in the dark city, and the watchmen are the people most likely to know what's out there.
Not warned, friend. She asks, “Have you seen the one I love?” She isn't asking about a warning. She just wants to know if anyone has spotted him.
Followed would make it sound like a chase. What she actually says is, “Have you seen the one I love?” Plain and hopeful, like asking a guard at the mall if they've seen your friend.
True! She says, “I had just passed them when I found the one I love.” The watchmen barely had time to answer, and there he was. All that searching and he's right there.
It's true, friend. She says, “I had just passed them when I found the one I love.” She hadn't gone far at all. The search ended right after she passed the watchmen.

She says, “I held him and would not let go until I had brought him to my mother's house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me.” She doesn't loosen her grip until he's home with her family. That's some determination.
No king's chambers in this verse. She says, “I held him and would not let go until I had brought him to my mother's house.” She takes him to the home where she came from.
En-gedi doesn't come up in this passage. She says she wouldn't let go “until I had brought him to my mother's house, to the chamber of the one who conceived me.” Her destination is her mother's home.

explanations.answer: Not to awaken love until the time is right
explanations.explanation: She says, “O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you by the gazelles and does of the field: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.” It's a solemn charge, and she means it. Love has a right time, and she asks them to wait for it.

explanations.answer: To help her search the city streets at night
explanations.explanation: Her search is over by now, friend. She found him, held him and brought him home. The charge to the daughters of Jerusalem is, “Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.”

explanations.answer: To keep her love a secret from everyone
explanations.explanation: Secrets aren't what she asks for. She says, “Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right.” The charge is about timing, not hiding.
